claim: Determination of the molecular properties of genetically targeted cell types has led to fundamental insights into mouse brain function and dysfunction.
source: Determination of the molecular properties of genetically targeted cell types has led to fundamental insights into mouse brain function and dysfunction.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific consensus about the utility of genetically targeted cell type analysis in mice.

claim: Classically defined, homologous neuronal and glial cell types differ between rodent and human by the expression of hundreds of orthologous, cell specific genes.
source: We demonstrate that classically defined, homologous neuronal and glial cell types differ between rodent and human by the expression of hundreds of orthologous, cell specific genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing differential expression analysis between species.

claim: Confirmation that these genes are differentially active was obtained using epigenetic mapping and immunofluorescence localization.
source: Confirmation that these genes are differentially active was obtained using epigenetic mapping and immunofluorescence localization.
evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq data and immunofluorescence experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Studies of sixteen human postmortem brains revealed gender specific transcriptional differences.
source: Studies of sixteen human postmortem brains revealed gender specific transcriptional differences, cell-specific molecular responses to aging, and the induction of a shared, robust response to an unknown external event evident in three donor samples.
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis comparing male and female samples in the manuscript.

claim: Studies of sixteen human postmortem brains revealed cell-specific molecular responses to aging.
source: Studies of sixteen human postmortem brains revealed gender specific transcriptional differences, cell-specific molecular responses to aging, and the induction of a shared, robust response to an unknown external event evident in three donor samples.
evidence: This claim is supported by age-related differential expression analysis in different cell types presented in the manuscript.

claim: Studies of sixteen human postmortem brains revealed the induction of a shared, robust response to an unknown external event evident in three donor samples.
source: Studies of sixteen human postmortem brains revealed gender specific transcriptional differences, cell-specific molecular responses to aging, and the induction of a shared, robust response to an unknown external event evident in three donor samples.
evidence: This claim is supported by principal component analysis and differential expression analysis identifying three samples with elevated immediate early gene expression.

claim: The ability to genetically target and molecularly profile specific cell types has begun to provide insight into essential features of the mammalian brain discovered by Ramon y Cajal over a century ago.
source: The ability to genetically target (Gong et al., 2003) and molecularly profile specific cell types (Heiman et al., 2008) has begun to provide insight into essential features of the mammalian brain that were discovered in the founding studies of Ramon y Cajal over a century ago (Cajal et al., 1899).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on genetic targeting and molecular profiling methods.

claim: Each anatomically distinct, classically defined cell type expresses a set of genes that is characteristic.
source: It has been established, for example, that each anatomically distinct, classically defined cell type expresses a set of genes that is characteristic (Dougherty et al., 2010; Doyle et al., 2008), that these genes confer properties that are essential for specialized cellular functions (Kim et al., 2008; Nakajima et al., 2014), and that the expression of these genes is highly correlated with cell specific epigenetic states that organize nuclear function (Kriaucionis and Heintz, 2009; Mellén et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous publications demonstrating cell-type specific gene expression.

claim: Cell-type specific genes confer properties that are essential for specialized cellular functions.
source: It has been established, for example, that each anatomically distinct, classically defined cell type expresses a set of genes that is characteristic (Dougherty et al., 2010; Doyle et al., 2008), that these genes confer properties that are essential for specialized cellular functions (Kim et al., 2008; Nakajima et al., 2014), and that the expression of these genes is highly correlated with cell specific epigenetic states that organize nuclear function (Kriaucionis and Heintz, 2009; Mellén et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous publications showing functional importance of cell-type specific genes.

claim: The expression of cell-type specific genes is highly correlated with cell specific epigenetic states that organize nuclear function.
source: It has been established, for example, that each anatomically distinct, classically defined cell type expresses a set of genes that is characteristic (Dougherty et al., 2010; Doyle et al., 2008), that these genes confer properties that are essential for specialized cellular functions (Kim et al., 2008; Nakajima et al., 2014), and that the expression of these genes is highly correlated with cell specific epigenetic states that organize nuclear function (Kriaucionis and Heintz, 2009; Mellén et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous publications demonstrating correlation between gene expression and epigenetic states.

claim: Environmental influences alter gene expression in affected cell types.
source: Application of these powerful new technologies in mouse models has also led to the realization that environmental influences (Heiman et al., 2008; Shrestha et al., 2015), internal physiological cues (Schmidt et al., 2012), and disease causing genetic lesions (Fyffe et al., 2008; Ingram et al., 2016) alter gene expression in affected cell types.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous publications showing environmental effects on gene expression.

claim: Internal physiological cues alter gene expression in affected cell types.
source: Application of these powerful new technologies in mouse models has also led to the realization that environmental influences (Heiman et al., 2008; Shrestha et al., 2015), internal physiological cues (Schmidt et al., 2012), and disease causing genetic lesions (Fyffe et al., 2008; Ingram et al., 2016) alter gene expression in affected cell types.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous publications showing physiological effects on gene expression.

claim: Disease causing genetic lesions alter gene expression in affected cell types.
source: Application of these powerful new technologies in mouse models has also led to the realization that environmental influences (Heiman et al., 2008; Shrestha et al., 2015), internal physiological cues (Schmidt et al., 2012), and disease causing genetic lesions (Fyffe et al., 2008; Ingram et al., 2016) alter gene expression in affected cell types.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous publications showing disease-related effects on gene expression.

claim: It is not known how many distinct cell types exist in the human brain.
source: It is not known, for instance, how many distinct cell types exist in the human brain, how these cell types vary between individuals or across species, whether the process of brain aging is equivalent between cell types, and why mutations in broadly expressed genes can have devastating consequences in one or a few select cell types.
evidence: This claim reflects a gap in current scientific knowledge about human brain cell type diversity.

claim: It is not known how cell types vary between individuals or across species.
source: It is not known, for instance, how many distinct cell types exist in the human brain, how these cell types vary between individuals or across species, whether the process of brain aging is equivalent between cell types, and why mutations in broadly expressed genes can have devastating consequences in one or a few select cell types.
evidence: This claim reflects a gap in current scientific knowledge about cell type variation.

claim: It is not known whether the process of brain aging is equivalent between cell types.
source: It is not known, for instance, how many distinct cell types exist in the human brain, how these cell types vary between individuals or across species, whether the process of brain aging is equivalent between cell types, and why mutations in broadly expressed genes can have devastating consequences in one or a few select cell types.
evidence: This claim reflects a gap in current scientific knowledge about cell-type specific aging.

claim: It is not known why mutations in broadly expressed genes can have devastating consequences in one or a few select cell types.
source: It is not known, for instance, how many distinct cell types exist in the human brain, how these cell types vary between individuals or across species, whether the process of brain aging is equivalent between cell types, and why mutations in broadly expressed genes can have devastating consequences in one or a few select cell types.
evidence: This claim reflects a gap in current scientific knowledge about cell-type specific disease mechanisms.

claim: Single cell gene expression profiling studies have been instrumental in providing an unbiased description of the diversity of cell types in the mouse and human brain.
source: The first involves gene expression profiling at the level of single cells (Darmanis et al., 2016; Macosko et al., 2015; Saunders et al., 2018; Thomsen et al., 2016; Zeisel et al., 2015) or single nuclei (Grindberg et al., 2013; Habib et al., 2016; Krishnaswami et al., 2016; Lacar et al., 2016; Lake et al., 2016). These studies have been instrumental in providing an unbiased description of the diversity of cell types and even subpopulations of cell types in the mouse and human brain.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple single cell sequencing studies.

claim: Profiles generated from single cell studies are highly variable due to technical challenges and transcriptional bursting.
source: However, the profiles generated from these studies are highly variable, both due to the technical challenge of amplifying signal from a small amount of starting material as well as biological mechanisms such as transcriptional bursting (Haque et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a publication discussing variability in single cell data.

claim: Single cell studies usually profile all cells from a tissue without enriching for cell types of interest, resulting in limited sequences for rare cell types.
source: Additionally, because single cell studies usually profile all cells from a tissue without enriching for cell types of interest, the vast majority of sequences generated from these studies will correspond to common cell types, with only limited sequences corresponding to rare cell types.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference about the nature of unbiased single cell profiling approaches.

claim: Neurons have complex cellular architecture, and techniques to achieve single cell suspension required for FACS stress and damage neurons.
source: Because neurons have complex cellular architecture, and techniques to achieve the single cell suspension required for FACS stress and damage neurons, an alternative strategy is to analyze isolated nuclei instead of whole cells (Matevossian and Akbarian, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and reflects established knowledge about neuronal fragility.

claim: Nuclear profiling methods have enabled transcriptional and epigenetic profiling of several cell types during development of both mouse and human brain.
source: These methods have enabled transcriptional and epigenetic profiling of several cell types during development of both the mouse and human brain (Ernst et al., 2014; Lister et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous publications using nuclear profiling methods.

claim: Only a few cell types have been characterized using nuclear profiling approaches, primarily due to difficulty identifying suitable antibodies.
source: However, only a few cell types have been characterized using this approach, primarily due to the difficulty of identifying antibodies to nuclear localized proteins that can label the nuclei from cell types of interest with sufficient specificity to enable sorting.
evidence: This claim reflects a limitation in previous nuclear profiling approaches based on available antibodies.

claim: The endoplasmic reticulum membrane is contiguous with the nuclear membrane.
source: To overcome this limitation, we have taken advantage of the fact that the endoplasmic reticulum membrane (ER) is contiguous with the nuclear membrane (Hetzer, 2010; Watson, 1955).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to publications describing ER-nuclear membrane continuity.

claim: Antibodies against both ER resident proteins and plasma membrane proteins being translated in the ER can be used for labeling and sorting nuclei from postmortem brains.
source: Here we demonstrate that antibodies against both ER resident proteins and plasma membrane proteins being translated in the ER can be used for labeling and sorting nuclei from postmortem brains, dramatically expanding the pool of antibodies available for cell specific nuclear isolation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing successful use of these antibodies for nuclear sorting.

claim: Nuclear RNA expression profiles can distinguish different cell types and reveal relationships between cell types.
source: Analysis of these data and published data for three cortical cell types (excitatory neurons, PV interneurons, and VIP interneurons, Mo et al. (2015) demonstrated that nuclear RNA expression profiles can both distinguish different cell types and reveal relationships between cell types (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: NeuN does not label Purkinje nuclei in cerebellar tissue sections.
source: However, both flow cytometry and imaging of the labeled nuclei yielded a surprising result: although NeuN is not known to label Purkinje nuclei in cerebellar tissue, staining of nuclei using NeuN robustly labels Purkinje nuclei (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim reflects established knowledge about NeuN staining patterns in tissue sections.

claim: Staining of isolated nuclei using NeuN robustly labels Purkinje nuclei.
source: However, both flow cytometry and imaging of the labeled nuclei yielded a surprising result: although NeuN is not known to label Purkinje nuclei in cerebellar tissue, staining of nuclei using NeuN robustly labels Purkinje nuclei (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry and imaging data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Exposure of antibody epitopes might be different between isolated nuclei and tissue sections.
source: Although we do observe lower levels of NeuN in labeled basket, astrocyte, and oligodendrocyte nuclei, this result suggests that exposure of antibody epitopes might be slightly different between isolated nuclei and tissue sections.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observed differences in NeuN staining between nuclei and tissue.

claim: The correlation between different cell types in the cerebellum is high (r = 0.91–0.94).
source: From this analysis, we could make several observations. First, the correlation between different cell types in the cerebellum is high: r = 0.91–0.94.
evidence: This claim is supported by Pearson correlation analysis of gene expression data.

claim: The correlation across biological replicates is very high (r = 0.98–1).
source: Second, the correlation across biological replicates is very high: r = 0.98–1.
evidence: This claim is supported by Pearson correlation analysis of biological replicates.

claim: There is very high correlation between genetically defined cell types and antibody defined cell types (r = 0.98 for granule cells and r = 0.99 for Purkinje cells).
source: Third, when we compared to the reference gene expression profiles from the EGFP-L10a labeled nuclei from granule cells, Purkinje cells, and Bergmann glia, we observed very high correlations between the genetically defined cell types and antibody defined cell types: r = 0.98 for granule cells and r = 0.99 for Purkinje cells; r = 0.96–0.97 between Bergmann glia purified from Sept4 EGFP-L10a animals and astrocytes purified via antibody labeling (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Bergmann glia are a sub-population of cerebellar astrocytes.
source: Since Bergmann glia are a sub-population of cerebellar astrocytes, it makes sense for these datasets to have slightly lower correlations.
evidence: This claim reflects established knowledge about the relationship between Bergmann glia and astrocytes.

claim: Hierarchical clustering separates samples according to cell class, with neuronal and glial samples separating from each other in the first split.
source: Fourth, when we perform hierarchical clustering, the samples cluster according to the cell class. Thus, neuronal and glial samples separate from each other in the first split.
evidence: This claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The five cell types separate from each other regardless of whether nuclei were purified using genetic labeling or antibody labeling.
source: The five cell types then separate from each other regardless of whether the nuclei were purified using genetic labeling (G) or antibody labeling (A).
evidence: This claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Antibody labeled samples undergo additional processing steps such as fixation but are highly similar to GFP-sorted samples.
source: Finally, although the antibody labeled samples undergo additional processing steps such as fixation, they are highly similar to the GFP-sorted samples in read distribution (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C—D) and gene expression (Figure 1G), suggesting that these technical differences have no or minimal effects on transcriptional profiles.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of read distribution and gene expression between antibody-labeled and GFP-sorted samples.

claim: The OLIG2+ population can be subdivided based on OLIG2 levels, with approximately 20% having high levels and 80% having lower levels.
source: By flow cytometry, we found that approximately 20% of all OLIG2+ nuclei have high levels OLIG2 (High) while 80% have lower levels (Low).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The OLIG2+ Low population contains mature oligodendrocytes, while OLIG2+ High nuclei contain a mix of mature oligodendrocytes and immature OPCs.
source: We found that both populations express general oligodendrocyte markers such as OLIG2, but that only OLIG2 +High nuclei express genes such as Pdgfra and Cspg4 that mark oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C). We conclude that the OLIG2+ Low population contains mature oligodendrocytes, while OLIG2+ High nuclei contain a mix of mature oligodendrocytes and immature OPCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq analysis of the two OLIG2+ populations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: OLIG2 levels are higher in oligodendrocyte precursors compared to mature oligodendrocytes.
source: This is consistent with previous studies demonstrating that OLIG2 levels are higher in oligodendrocyte precursors compared to mature oligodendrocytes (Hayashi et al., 2011; Kitada and Rowitch, 2006; Kuhlmann et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous publications showing differential OLIG2 expression.

claim: Fluorescence activated nuclear sorting can be used to identify subpopulations of cell types.
source: These results indicate that fluorescence activated nuclear sorting can also be used to identify subpopulations of cell types.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the successful identification of OPC and mature oligodendrocyte subpopulations.

claim: Population-based cell type specific profiling outperforms single nuclei sequencing in the number of genes detected regardless of sequencing depth.
source: In particular, the ability to selectively isolate populations of interest allows for efficient profiling of rare cell types without the need to extensively profile common cell types. Additionally, when we compared our cerebellar glial datasets to published sequencing results from hippocampal glial single nuclei (Habib et al., 2016), we found that our methodology outperforms single nuclei sequencing in the number of genes detected regardless of sequencing depth (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D-E), and that the expression of general or cell-type specific genes is more variable across single nuclei samples than in our biological replicates (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of gene detection between methods shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D-E.

claim: Expression of general or cell-type specific genes is more variable across single nuclei samples than in biological replicates of population-based profiling.
source: Additionally, when we compared our cerebellar glial datasets to published sequencing results from hippocampal glial single nuclei (Habib et al., 2016), we found that our methodology outperforms single nuclei sequencing in the number of genes detected regardless of sequencing depth (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D-E), and that the expression of general or cell-type specific genes is more variable across single nuclei samples than in our biological replicates (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of gene expression variability shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F.

claim: The staining profiles of rat nuclei resemble those of mouse.
source: Nuclei were isolated from rat cerebellum, fixed and stained using the same antibodies that we used in mouse, and the results were analyzed on a flow cytometer (Figure 2A). The staining profiles of rat nuclei resembled those of mouse (Figure 1B), although there were differences.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of flow cytometry data from rat and mouse shown in Figures 2A and 1B.

claim: In the rat cerebellum, NeuN staining resulted in better separated positive and negative populations than in the mouse cerebellum.
source: For example, in the rat cerebellum, NeuN staining resulted in better separated positive and negative populations than was evident in the mouse cerebellum.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of flow cytometry data from rat and mouse.

claim: It was possible to isolate nuclei from basket cells, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes by staining with antibodies against SORCS3 and NeuN in rat.
source: Purification and analysis of these populations by RNA-seq revealed that some cell types could be isolated using more than one sorting strategy. For example, we found that it was possible to isolate nuclei from basket cells, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes by staining with antibodies against SORCS3 and NeuN.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq analysis of populations sorted using different antibody combinations.

claim: For the top 20 most specific genes for all rat cell types, labeling specifically in the defined cell type is observed on average 93% of the time in the Allen Mouse Brain Atlas.
source: For the top 20 most specific genes for all cell types, we observe labeling specifically in the defined cell type on average 93% of the time.
evidence: This claim is supported by validation of rat-specific genes using the Allen Mouse Brain Atlas in situ hybridization database.

claim: The conditions used to sort granule and basket neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and OPCs were directly transferrable to human postmortem tissue.
source: Although the profile of stained human cerebellar nuclei is generally similar to rodent, there are differences (Figure 2C). For example, the conditions used to sort granule and basket neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and OPCs were directly transferrable to human postmortem tissue, whereas those used to sort mouse and rat Purkinje cell nuclei were not successful for isolation of human Purkinje cell nuclei, possibly because while Purkinje cells are already rare in mouse and rat (0.1% in mouse, 0.05% in rat; Figures 1B and 2A), they have been reported to be even more rare in human (Korbo and Andersen, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data from human samples shown in Figure 2C and comparison with rodent data.

claim: Purkinje cells are rare in mouse (0.1%) and rat (0.05%).
source: For example, the conditions used to sort granule and basket neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and OPCs were directly transferrable to human postmortem tissue, whereas those used to sort mouse and rat Purkinje cell nuclei were not successful for isolation of human Purkinje cell nuclei, possibly because while Purkinje cells are already rare in mouse and rat (0.1% in mouse, 0.05% in rat; Figures 1B and 2A), they have been reported to be even more rare in human (Korbo and Andersen, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing Purkinje cell percentages in Figures 1B and 2A.

claim: Purkinje cells have been reported to be even more rare in human than in rodents.
source: For example, the conditions used to sort granule and basket neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and OPCs were directly transferrable to human postmortem tissue, whereas those used to sort mouse and rat Purkinje cell nuclei were not successful for isolation of human Purkinje cell nuclei, possibly because while Purkinje cells are already rare in mouse and rat (0.1% in mouse, 0.05% in rat; Figures 1B and 2A), they have been reported to be even more rare in human (Korbo and Andersen, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a publication reporting Purkinje cell rarity in human.

claim: The two neuronal cell types (granule and basket) were highly correlated between human samples (r = 0.99 for both).
source: Calculation of pairwise Pearson correlation coefficients across the ten datasets revealed that the two neuronal cell types (granule and basket) were highly correlated between samples (r = 0.99 for both), while the glial data had slightly lower correlations (r = 0.96–0.97).
evidence: This claim is supported by Pearson correlation analysis of human cell type data.

claim: Glial data from human samples had slightly lower correlations (r = 0.96–0.97) than neuronal data.
source: Calculation of pairwise Pearson correlation coefficients across the ten datasets revealed that the two neuronal cell types (granule and basket) were highly correlated between samples (r = 0.99 for both), while the glial data had slightly lower correlations (r = 0.96–0.97).
evidence: This claim is supported by Pearson correlation analysis of human cell type data.

claim: Hierarchical clustering of human samples resulted in separation by cell type, indicating that variation across cell types is stronger than between individual samples.
source: Hierarchical clustering resulted in separation of the samples by cell type, indicating that the variation across cell types is stronger than that between individual samples (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: When hierarchical clustering was performed using all genes, samples resolved primarily by species.
source: To explore the similarities and differences across species, we used hierarchical clustering to determine the relationships between samples. Interestingly, we found that when we performed clustering using all genes, the samples resolved primarily by species (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: When hierarchical clustering was performed using the 250 most variable genes, samples clustered primarily by cell type.
source: However, when we performed clustering using the 250 most variable genes across samples, they clustered primarily by the cell type (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The range of correlation coefficients between samples for the same cell type across species is similar to that for cell types isolated from the same species.
source: To further investigate this result, we computed the pairwise Pearson correlation coefficients across all samples (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C). We found that the range of correlation coefficients between the samples for the same cell type across species is similar to that for cell types isolated from the same species, suggesting that both cell type and species are important determinants of the expression profiles.
evidence: This claim is supported by Pearson correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Both cell type and species are important determinants of expression profiles.
source: We found that the range of correlation coefficients between the samples for the same cell type across species is similar to that for cell types isolated from the same species, suggesting that both cell type and species are important determinants of the expression profiles.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from correlation analysis of gene expression data.

claim: PC1 and 3 categorize samples by cell type, while PC2, 6, and 8 split samples by species.
source: Examination of the first eight principal components (PC1-8), which collectively account for 90.5% of the variability across all samples, revealed that PC1 and 3 categorize samples by the cell type, while PC2, 6, and 8 split samples by species.
evidence: This claim is supported by principal components analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D-F.

claim: PC1 and 3 account for 47% of the variability across samples while PC2, 6, and 8 account for only 22% of variability.
source: Because PC1 and 3 account for 47% of the variability across samples while PC2, 6, and 8 account for only 22% of variability (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), we conclude that the most important differences between the profiles result from the cell-type specific expressed genes that are shared among species, but that some important differences also arise due to the expression of species-specific genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by principal components analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The most important differences between profiles result from cell-type specific expressed genes that are shared among species, but some important differences also arise due to expression of species-specific genes.
source: Because PC1 and 3 account for 47% of the variability across samples while PC2, 6, and 8 account for only 22% of variability (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), we conclude that the most important differences between the profiles result from the cell-type specific expressed genes that are shared among species, but that some important differences also arise due to the expression of species-specific genes.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from principal components analysis of gene expression data.

claim: Between 70 and 280 cell-type and species specific differentially expressed genes were identified that were approximately equally distributed between those enriched in mouse and those enriched in human.
source: Filtering in this way yielded between 70 and 280 cell-type and species specific differentially expressed genes that were approximately equally distributed between those enriched in mouse and those enriched in human (Figure 3B, S5B, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 3B and Supplementary file 4.

claim: Expression of species-enriched genes in rat most often resembles expression in mouse.
source: Interestingly, expression of these genes in rat most often resembles expression in mouse (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of gene expression in rat shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Expression of human-enriched genes in human single nuclei data is significantly higher than expression of mouse-enriched genes for all cell types.
source: We found that for all cell types and for both measures of expression, the expression of human-enriched genes in human single nuclei data is significantly higher than the expression of mouse-enriched genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of single nuclei data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Expression of mouse-enriched genes in mouse single cell data is higher than expression of human-enriched genes for all cell types, including subpopulations.
source: Concordantly, the expression of mouse-enriched genes in mouse single cell data is higher than the expression of human-enriched genes for all cell types, including subpopulations of each cell type (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of single cell data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3D.

claim: The distributions of expression for mouse- and human-enriched genes are statistically different for all cell types except OPCs.
source: For both measures of expression, the distributions of expression for mouse- and human-enriched genes are statistically different for all cell types except for OPCs, which is likely due to sample size as Saunders et al. only identified eight cerebellar OPCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of single cell/nuclei data.

claim: The genes identified as differentially expressed between human and mouse are likely to be true species differences and do not arise from sorting different subpopulations in the two species.
source: These results confirm that the genes we have identified as differentially expressed between human and mouse are likely to be true species differences, and do not arise as a result of sorting different subpopulations in the two species.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from validation using single cell/nuclei data.

claim: GO analysis of human-enriched genes from granule neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and OPCs do not have significantly associated GO categories.
source: GO analysis of human-enriched genes from granule neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and OPCs do not have significantly associated GO categories, suggesting species differences in these cell types contribute to a wide range of pathways and functions.
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis results.

claim: The majority of human-enriched genes in basket cells are functionally unrelated, although there was significant enrichment for the cellular component sub-ontology cell projection membrane.
source: The majority of human-enriched genes in basket cells are also unrelated functionally, although there was significant enrichment for the cellular component sub-ontology cell projection membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis results.

claim: GO analysis of mouse-enriched genes from astrocytes revealed weak enrichment for genes with phosphoric diester hydrolase/phospholipase activity.
source: GO analysis of mouse-enriched genes from astrocytes revealed weak enrichment for genes with phosphoric diester hydrolase/phospholipase activity, while mouse-enriched genes from granule neurons, basket neurons, oligodendrocytes, and OPCs revealed enrichment for genes with transporter activity or those involved in neuronal development (Supplementary file 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis results in Supplementary file 9.

claim: Mouse-enriched genes from granule neurons, basket neurons, oligodendrocytes, and OPCs revealed enrichment for genes with transporter activity or those involved in neuronal development.
source: GO analysis of mouse-enriched genes from astrocytes revealed weak enrichment for genes with phosphoric diester hydrolase/phospholipase activity, while mouse-enriched genes from granule neurons, basket neurons, oligodendrocytes, and OPCs revealed enrichment for genes with transporter activity or those involved in neuronal development (Supplementary file 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis results in Supplementary file 9.

claim: Evolutionary divergence between mouse and human cell types involves both frequent alterations in regulatory mechanisms impacting single genes and those regulating conserved, functionally important pathways.
source: These data indicate that evolutionary divergence between mouse and human cell types involves both frequent alterations in regulatory mechanisms impacting single genes (Villar et al., 2015), and those regulating conserved, functionally important pathways (Nord et al., 2015; Rebeiz et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from GO analysis results and is supported by citations to relevant publications.

claim: The Allen Mouse Brain Atlas and GENSAT Project demonstrate expression in the granule layer of the cerebellum for the mouse-enriched genes Cnksr3, Ece1, and Pde1c.
source: These data demonstrate expression in the granule layer of the cerebellum for the mouse-enriched genes Cnksr3, Ece1, and Pde1c, and the absence of expression of the human-enriched genes Ccdc175, Clvs2, Vwc2, and Pde1a (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by validation using Allen Mouse Brain Atlas and GENSAT data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The Allen Mouse Brain Atlas and GENSAT Project demonstrate absence of expression of the human-enriched genes Ccdc175, Clvs2, Vwc2, and Pde1a in mouse cerebellum.
source: These data demonstrate expression in the granule layer of the cerebellum for the mouse-enriched genes Cnksr3, Ece1, and Pde1c, and the absence of expression of the human-enriched genes Ccdc175, Clvs2, Vwc2, and Pde1a (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by validation using Allen Mouse Brain Atlas and GENSAT data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Clvs2 and Pde1a are expressed in other regions in the mouse brain, suggesting that alterations in cell specific regulatory sequences may underlie species differences.
source: Interestingly, while Clvs2 and Pde1a are absent from the cerebellum, they are expressed in other regions in the mouse brain, suggesting that alterations in cell specific regulatory sequences may underlie these species differences (Carroll, 2005; Carroll, 2008).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from expression data and is supported by citations to relevant publications.

claim: The majority of ATAC peaks in the samples are located in promoters or gene bodies.
source: The majority of ATAC peaks in our samples are located in promoters or gene bodies (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq peak distribution analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Protein coding genes that are identified as expressed have ATAC peaks in their promoters and gene bodies.
source: As expected, protein coding genes that are identified as expressed in our data have ATAC peaks in their promoters and gene bodies.
evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq data analysis.

claim: In human granule cells, JKAMP, CCDC175, and RTN1 are all expressed at significant levels with primary transcripts over the gene body and ATAC peaks at the promoter.
source: In human granule cells, all three genes are expressed at significant levels, as is evident by the presence of primary transcripts over the gene body, and ATAC peaks at the promoter (Figure 4A - top).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In mouse granule cells, expression of the Rtn1 gene is conserved with similar levels of nuclear transcripts and promoter ATAC coverage as in human.
source: In mouse granule cells, expression of the Rtn1 gene [1] is conserved, with similar levels of nuclear transcripts (7.6 log2(normalized counts) in human vs 8.1 in mouse) and promoter ATAC coverage (2.6 log2(FPKM) in mouse vs 2.9 in human).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data between human and mouse.

claim: No primary transcripts and no promoter ATAC peaks are observed for the mouse Ccdc175 gene.
source: In to contrast the robust expression of the CCDC175 gene [2] evident in human granule cells, no primary transcripts and no promoter ATAC peaks are observed for the mouse gene (we did not quantify expression or ATAC coverage for CCDC175 because the mouse and human genes are annotated as low confidence orthologs and thus excluded from quantitative analysis).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data.

claim: Jkamp is expressed in both human and mouse granule neurons, but its expression in mouse is reduced approximately five-fold and the accessibility of its promoter is reduced.
source: The third gene in this locus Jkamp [1], is an intermediate case. Although Jkamp is expressed in both human and mouse granule neurons, its expression in mouse is reduced approximately five-fold (8.6 log2(normalized counts) in human vs 6.3 in mouse) and the accessibility of its promoter is reduced (ATAC coverage 3.8 log2(FPKM) in human vs 1.7 in mouse).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data between human and mouse.

claim: In mouse, most of 109 mouse-enriched granule cell genes have strong promoter ATAC signals compared to only a few of the 101 human-enriched genes.
source: In mouse, the reverse is true – most of 109 mouse-enriched genes have strong promoter ATAC signals compared to only a few of the 101 human-enriched genes (Figure 4B – right).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In human, the majority of the 147 human-enriched basket cell genes have strong ATAC signal over the promoter region, while only a few of the 133 mouse-enriched genes have strong ATAC signals.
source: In human, the majority of the 147 human-enriched genes have strong ATAC signal over the promoter region, while only a few of the 133 mouse-enriched genes have strong ATAC signals (Figure 4C – left); in mouse, the reverse is true (Figure 4C – right).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: DNA bases contained within ATAC peaks associated with mouse- or human-enriched genes are less conserved than those associated with housekeeping genes.
source: We found that DNA bases contained within ATAC peaks associated with mouse- or human-enriched genes are less conserved than those associated with housekeeping genes (Figure 4D, left for granule cells, right for basket cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by PhastCons conservation score analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The centers of defined ATAC peaks are more conserved compared to the beginning or end of peaks, and this difference is more prominent for housekeeping genes than for human- or mouse-enriched genes.
source: Analysis of conservation scores over the normalized length of promoter ATAC peaks reveals that while the centers of defined peaks are more conserved compared to the beginning or end of peaks, this difference is more prominent for housekeeping genes that for human- or mouse-enriched genes (Figure 4E, left for granule cells, right for basket cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by conservation score analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Differences in expression of cell-type and species-specific genes between human and mouse might result from evolutionary driven differences in promoter chromatin accessibility.
source: These results suggest that differences we observe in the expression of cell-type and species-specific genes between human and mouse might result from evolutionary driven differences in promoter chromatin accessibility between the two species.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from conservation and ATAC-seq data analysis.

claim: Mouse granule cells express only Pde1c, whereas granule cells from human express high levels of PDE1A and low levels of PDE1C.
source: Our data demonstrate that mouse granule cells express only Pde1c, whereas granule cells from human express high levels of PDE1A and low levels of PDE1C (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: PDE1A is expressed in the human but not mouse cerebellum.
source: Our results match previous findings that PDE1A is expressed in the human but not mouse cerebellum (Loughney and Ferguson, 1996; Loughney et al., 1996; Sonnenburg et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous publications and is confirmed by the current data.

claim: Both PDE1A and PDE1C are primarily localized in the granule layer, with PDE1C expression predominant in mouse and PDE1A expression predominant in human cerebellum.
source: We found, consistent with the RNA-seq and ATAC data, that both PDE1 members are primarily localized in the granule layer, with PDE1C expression predominant in mouse and PDE1A expression predominant in human cerebellum (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: PDE1A preferentially hydrolyzes cGMP while PDE1C hydrolyzes both cAMP and cGMP with equal efficiencies.
source: Since PDE1A preferentially hydrolyzes cGMP while PDE1C hydrolyzes both cAMP and cGMP with equal efficiencies (Takimoto, 2009), these differences in gene expression may result in changes in neuronal activity between granule cells from the two species.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a publication describing PDE1 enzyme properties.

claim: Differences in PDE1 gene expression may result in changes in neuronal activity between granule cells from mouse and human.
source: Since PDE1A preferentially hydrolyzes cGMP while PDE1C hydrolyzes both cAMP and cGMP with equal efficiencies (Takimoto, 2009), these differences in gene expression may result in changes in neuronal activity between granule cells from the two species.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from known enzyme properties and observed expression differences.

claim: Trps1, which encodes an atypical GATA factor that specifically binds to the consensus GATA sequence, is expressed in granule cells in mouse but not human.
source: However, we found that Trps1, which encodes an atypical GATA factor that has been shown to specifically bind to the consensus GATA sequence (Malik et al., 2001), is expressed in granule cells in mouse but not human (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and a citation describing TRPS1 binding properties.

claim: Human mutations in the GATA binding domain of TRPS1 cause defects in bone development, but these phenotypes are not completely recapitulated in the mouse model.
source: A previous study has found that while human mutations in the GATA binding domain of TRPS1 cause defects in bone development, these phenotypes are not completely recapitulated in the mouse model (Malik et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a publication describing TRPS1 mutations and mouse models.

claim: Changes in the pattern of transcription factor expression between mouse and human may contribute to discrepancies in phenotypes between mouse models and human disease.
source: Although there are no reports of neurological phenotypes in the mosue model, our results suggest that changes in the pattern of transcription factor expression between mouse and human may contribute to discrepancies in phenotypes between mouse models and human disease.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from observed expression differences and known phenotypic discrepancies.

claim: Gene expression in the brain is highly conserved in specific cell types across species.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that nuclear RNA-seq data can be employed to accurately assess cell-type specific gene expression in rodent and human brain, and they allow several important conclusions regarding gene expression in the nervous system. First, gene expression in the brain is highly conserved in specific cell types across species.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the high correlation of gene expression between species for the same cell types.

claim: Most abundant and cell-specific markers of well characterized cell types are shared between rodent and human brain.
source: Accordingly, most abundant and cell-specific markers of well characterized cell types are shared between rodent and human brain.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that known markers are expressed in corresponding cell types across species.

claim: Despite shared identity, there are a significant number of genes in each cell type whose expression is not conserved between species.
source: Second, despite this shared identity, there are a significant number of genes in each cell type whose expression is not conserved between species.
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis identifying hundreds of species-enriched genes.

claim: Species-enriched genes do not generally conform to known GO categories, and in some cases, they are expressed in other brain regions.
source: This group of genes does not generally conform to known GO categories, and in some cases, they are expressed in other brain regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis results and validation using brain atlas data.

claim: Cell-type and species-specific expression can reflect altered regulation of adjacent genes within a locus, or selective expression of functionally related yet distinct members of a given gene family.
source: Third, cell-type and species-specific expression can reflect altered regulation of adjacent genes within a locus, or selective expression of functionally related yet distinct members of a given gene family.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from examples like the JKAMP/CCDC175/RTN1 locus and PDE1 family members.

claim: Cell-type specific changes in the expression of transcription factors may impact the expression of downstream genes.
source: Finally, cell-type specific changes in the expression of transcription factors may impact the expression of downstream genes.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation of differential TRPS1 expression and enrichment of GATA motifs.

claim: Important differences in gene expression in specific CNS cell types occur between species and may result in functionally important differences in biochemical functions.
source: Although the consequences of these gene expression changes will have to be interrogated in future studies, our data demonstrate that important differences in gene expression in specific CNS cell types occur between species and suggest that they may result in functionally important differences in the biochemical functions of even the most classically defined rodent and human cell types.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observed gene expression differences and their potential functional implications.

claim: 767 and 1381 SNPs from the NHGRI-EBI GWAS catalog are located in accessible regions associated with granule and basket neurons respectively.
source: We found 767 and 1381 SNPs that are located in accessible regions associated with granule and basket neurons respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by overlap analysis of GWAS SNPs with ATAC-seq peaks.

claim: 163 and 363 SNPs are located in regions that are differentially accessible in granule and basket neurons.
source: Of these, 163 and 363 SNPs are located in regions that are differentially accessible in granule and basket neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by overlap analysis of GWAS SNPs with differentially accessible ATAC-seq peaks.

claim: Many SNPs in SNCA have been strongly associated with both familial and sporadic Parkinson's disease.
source: For example, while many SNPs in SNCA, the gene that encodes alpha-synuclein, have been strongly associated with both familial and sporadic Parkinson's disease (Campêlo and Silva, 2017; Stefanis, 2012), less is known about the mechanism by which non-coding SNPs in SNCA contribute to disease risk.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to publications describing SNCA SNP associations with Parkinson's disease.

claim: SNCA is expressed at higher levels in granule neurons relative to basket neurons.
source: We found that SNCA is expressed at higher levels in granule neurons relative to basket neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E); correspondingly, we identified seven regions around the SNCA gene that are preferentially accessible in granule neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E) and may regulate SNCA expression in cis.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Seven regions around the SNCA gene are preferentially accessible in granule neurons and may regulate SNCA expression in cis.
source: We found that SNCA is expressed at higher levels in granule neurons relative to basket neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E); correspondingly, we identified seven regions around the SNCA gene that are preferentially accessible in granule neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E) and may regulate SNCA expression in cis.
evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E and involves speculation about regulatory function.

claim: Putative regulatory regions around SNCA contain two SNPs (rs356182 and rs2736990) that have been linked to Parkinson's disease.
source: These putative regulatory regions contain two SNPs that have previously been linked to Parkinson's - rs356182 and rs2736990.
evidence: This claim is supported by overlap of ATAC-seq peaks with GWAS SNPs.

claim: The GG genotype of rs356182 has been associated with a tremor-dominant, slower-progressing form of Parkinson's and with lower levels of SNCA expression in the cerebellum but not in other brain regions.
source: Interestingly, the GG genotype of rs356182, which has been associated with a tremor-dominant, slower-progressing form of Parkinson's, is also associated with lower levels of SNCA expression in the cerebellum but not in any other brain regions including substantia nigra, caudate, and frontal cortex (Cooper et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a publication describing rs356182 associations.

claim: Samples were obtained from 16 control donors, roughly equally split between genders (seven males and nine females), and across ages (four individuals each in age groups: 20–30, 40–50, 60–70, 80–90 years).
source: In total, we obtained samples from 16 control donors, roughly equally split between genders (seven males and nine females), and across ages (four individuals each in the following age groups: 20–30, 40–50, 60–70, 80–90 years) (Figures 2C and 5A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by sample information shown in Figures 2C and 5A and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Pairwise Pearson correlation coefficients between biological replicates for each cell type are between 0.98 and 1.
source: Pairwise Pearson correlation coefficients between biological replicates for each cell type are between 0.98 and 1 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Despite differences between individuals in the abundance of each cell type or the recovery of nuclei during preparation and sorting, the cell-type specific human expression data obtained by nuclear sorting is highly reproducible.
source: These data demonstrate that, despite differences between individuals in the abundance of each cell type or the recovery of nuclei during preparation and sorting, the cell-type specific human expression data obtained by nuclear sorting is highly reproducible.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the high correlation between biological replicates.

claim: Only a few genes significantly change with postmortem delay: 12 across all samples, four in granule cells, one in basket cells, and one in glia.
source: We found that only a few genes significantly change with PMD: 12 across all samples, four in granule cells, one in basket cells, and one in glia (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis with PMD as a covariate.

claim: Only one gene (KIF19 in glia) changed linearly with postmortem delay.
source: Examination of these genes revealed that only one, KIF19 in glia, changed linearly with PMD (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by examination of gene expression versus PMD shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Autolysis has a relatively minor effect on expression data obtained from post-mortem human tissue.
source: These data confirm an earlier report that autolysis has a relatively minor effect on expression data obtained from post-mortem human tissue (Gupta et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by the current data and a citation to a previous publication.

claim: Of the 27 genes exhibiting gender-specific differential expression, seven are located on the X chromosome, 14 are on the Y chromosome, and six on autosomes.
source: Of the 27 genes exhibiting gender-specific differential expression (adjusted p-value<0.01, baseMean >50), seven are located on the X chromosome, 14 are on the Y chromosome, and six on autosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis comparing males and females.

claim: GYG2P1 is a male-enriched gene across all samples and is more male-enriched in basket cells than granule cells and glia.
source: For example, we identified Glycogenin 2 Pseudogene 1 (GYG2P1) as a male-enriched gene across all samples, although it is clearly more male-enriched in basket cells than granule cells and glia (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis and visualization shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The Y chromosome locus containing GYG2P1 shows male-specific basket cell expression across a large region, including GYG2P1 and approximately 300 kb downstream.
source: Examination of the Y chromosome locus containing GYG2P1 reveals male-specific basket cell expression across a large region, including GYG2P1 and approximately 300 kb downstream (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: 274 genes significantly change with age in granule cells, 139 in basket cells, 31 in glia, and 42 across all samples regardless of cell type.
source: We found 274 significant genes in granule cells, 139 in basket cells, 31 in glia, and 42 that are significant across all samples regardless of cell type (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis with age as a covariate.

claim: Aging genes are about equally split between those that increase in expression and those that decrease in expression with age.
source: These genes are about equally split between those that increase in expression and those that decrease in expression with age (Figure 6C, S9G).
evidence: This claim is supported by visualization of aging genes shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Only a few genes significantly change with age in more than one cell type.
source: Interestingly, only a few genes significantly change with age in more than one cell type.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of aging genes across cell types.

claim: The 42 genes that are identified as significantly changed with age across all cell types appear heterogeneous, and most do not reach significance when tested in each cell type individually.
source: For example, the 42 genes that are identified as significantly changed with age across all cell types appear heterogeneous (Figure 6C), and most of these do not reach significance when tested in each cell type individually (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The Pearson's correlation between age and expression of the 274 granule aging genes in granule neurons is 0.76, but only 0.42 and 0.32 when expression of these genes is examined in basket neurons and glia.
source: For example, the Pearson's correlation between age and the expression of the 274 granule aging genes in granule neurons is 0.76, but only 0.42 and 0.32 when expression of these genes is examined in basket neurons and glia.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1H.

claim: The specific molecular consequences of aging, at least in the cerebellum, are different between cell types.
source: These data suggest that the specific molecular consequences of aging, at least in the cerebellum, are different between cell types.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that different genes change with age in different cell types.

claim: Genes down-regulated with age in all three individual cell types are enriched for synaptic genes.
source: However, we found that the genes down-regulated with age in all three individual cell types, despite containing different specific genes, were enriched for synaptic genes (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: The finding that genes encoding synaptic components decline in expression with age is consistent with previous findings that axons and dendrites atrophy in the brains of older individuals.
source: Our finding that genes encoding synaptic components decline in expression with age is consistent with previous findings that axons and dendrites atrophy in the brains of older individuals (Burke and Barnes, 2006; Dickstein et al., 2013; Freeman et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by the current data and citations to previous publications describing age-related brain changes.

claim: Age-related decline in synaptic gene expression impacts distinct genes in each cell type.
source: However, our data extend these observations to establish that this general process impacts distinct genes in each cell type, as might be expected from the distinct protein compositions of synapses or synapse-related functions in each cell type.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that different synaptic genes decline in different cell types.

claim: A deeper understanding of neurological aging requires examination of defined cell types rather than whole tissue.
source: Although further studies are necessary to determine whether these principles hold for other regions of the brain, our findings argue that a deeper understanding of neurological aging requires examination of defined cell types rather than whole tissue.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the cell-type specific nature of aging-related gene expression changes.

claim: The first principal component for all cell types splits the samples based on gender.
source: We found that while the first principal component for all cell types splits the samples based on gender, the second principle component for granule cells and glia splits three donors (WI, VM, and ZH) away from the other 13 (Figure 7B, right panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by principal components analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The second principal component for granule cells and glia splits three donors (WI, VM, and ZH) away from the other 13.
source: We found that while the first principal component for all cell types splits the samples based on gender, the second principle component for granule cells and glia splits three donors (WI, VM, and ZH) away from the other 13 (Figure 7B, right panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by principal components analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The genes that contribute most to PC2 separation in granule and glia samples include immediate early genes FOS, FOSB, and NPAS4 as well as heat shock genes HSPA1A and HSPB1.
source: Examination of the loading vectors for PC2 from granule and glia samples shows the genes that contribute the most to the separation of these three donors include the immediate early genes FOS, FOSB, and NPAS4 as well as heat shock genes HSPA1A and HSPB1 (Figure 7B, left panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by principal components analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In granule cells, samples WI, VM, and ZH are characterized by the induction of 224 genes and diminished expression of 10 genes.
source: In granule cells, samples WI, VM, and ZH are characterized by the induction of 224 genes and diminished expression of 10 genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis comparing the three samples to others.

claim: An overlapping but weaker response that included 136 induced genes was present in glial cells from samples WI, VM, and ZH.
source: An overlapping but weaker response that included 136 induced genes was present in glial cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis of glial samples.

claim: The induction of genes in glia from samples WI, VM, and ZH is not due to contamination by granule cells.
source: The induction of these genes in glia is not due to contamination by granule cells as highly expressed markers for granule cells (e.g. FAT2) are not present in the glial data (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by examination of cell-type marker expression shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Only two differentially expressed genes were evident in the basket cell data from samples WI, VM, and ZH.
source: Only two differentially expressed genes were evident in the basket cell data.
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis of basket cell samples.

claim: Out of 560 combinations partitioning 16 individuals into groups of three and thirteen, 529 resulted in fewer than 50 differentially expressed genes, and only five resulted in greater than 234 differentially expressed genes.
source: Out of the 560 combinations, 529 resulted in fewer than 50 differentially expressed genes, and only five resulted in greater than 234 differentially expressed genes (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by resampling analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The five combinations that resulted in greater than 234 differentially expressed genes all contain groups of three young or old individuals, suggesting that the differentially expressed genes reflect a real biological difference in age-associated genes.
source: These five combinations all contain groups of three young or old individuals, suggesting that the differentially expressed genes reflect a real biological difference in age-associated genes (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from resampling analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: GO analysis of the 224 granule cell induced genes revealed categories associated with protein folding and response to heat.
source: GO analysis of the 224 granule cell induced genes revealed categories associated with protein folding and response to heat (Figure 7D, Supplementary file 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 7D and Supplementary file 9.

claim: Induction of immediate early genes EGR1, FOS, and FOSB occurs in samples WI, VM, and ZH, but no difference in expression of ARC is evident.
source: Analysis of the expression of immediate early genes, which are associated with neuronal activation (Okuno, 2011; Pérez-Cadahía et al., 2011), indicated that their induction is also selective. For example, induction of EGR1, FOS, and FOSB occurs, but no difference in expression of ARC (a well-characterized immediate early gene) is evident (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by examination of immediate early gene expression shown in Figure 7E.

claim: There is no evidence for induction of glial genes such as GFAP and S100B that mark astrocyte activation in response to stroke and other forms of damage in samples WI, VM, and ZH.
source: Furthermore, although expression of immediate early genes such as c-FOS can become induced in response to damage such as ischemic stroke, we found no evidence for induction of glial genes such as GFAP and S100B that mark astrocyte activation in response to stroke and other forms of damage (Choudhury and Ding, 2016; Ding, 2014; Dirnagl et al., 1999; Kajihara et al., 2001; Pekny and Nilsson, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by examination of astrocyte activation marker expression and citations to relevant publications.

claim: Examination of clinical records failed to reveal features (gender, age, PMD, cause of death) that distinguished the three samples WI, VM, and ZH from the 13 other control donors.
source: Finally, examination of the clinical records failed to reveal features (gender, age, PMD, cause of death) that distinguished these three samples from the 13 other control donors.
evidence: This claim is supported by examination of clinical metadata.

claim: Nuclear expression profiling of specific cell types can be used to discover pathways and biomarkers.
source: Although the cause or causes of these molecular events remain obscure, the discovery of this strong and highly reproducible response in select postmortem human brain samples indicates that nuclear expression profiling of specific cell types can be used to discover pathways and biomarkers.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the discovery of the robust molecular response in three samples.

claim: Further work is required to determine whether the pathways and biomarkers identified are associated with human physiological conditions, agonal factors, or technical differences in tissue processing.
source: Further work is required to determine whether these pathways and biomarkers are associated with human physiological conditions, whether they reflect agonal factors prior to death or technical differences in tissue processing post mortem.
evidence: This claim acknowledges uncertainty about the cause of the observed molecular response.
